judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 364. It widens the ban on paddling students with disabilities. Corporal punishment means causing pain on purpose, such as hitting, paddling or spanking. The old law barred school staff from doing this to only some students. It covered students with the most severe thinking and learning disabilities. Even then, it applied only if the student's yearly school plan said so. The act now covers any student who has a disability under federal special education law. It also deletes a rule that let a parent sign a form allowing the punishment anyway. A yes vote was a vote to widen the ban and drop that parent form. The Oklahoma House passed it 63-25. It became law without the Governor's signature.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 504. It ends marriage before the age of eighteen. Before the act, someone under eighteen could marry if a parent or guardian agreed. Someone under sixteen could marry if a judge agreed. A judge could agree in two cases. One was to settle a court case over paternity. The other was where the girl was pregnant or had given birth. The act deletes all of that. Now only a person who is at least eighteen may marry. The rule against marrying a close relative stays. The Oklahoma House passed it 51-36. It became law without the Governor's signature.

judgments.yea_description: Voted to override the Governor's veto of House Bill 2263. It bans holding a phone while driving through a school zone or a work zone. The ban is narrow. It applies only while the car is moving in a marked school zone with a lower speed limit in force, or in a road work zone. There a driver may not hold or use a hand-held phone. The driver may not type, send or read a text. Hands-free use is still allowed. So is calling for help in an emergency. The fine is up to one hundred dollars, and the state may not add points to the driver's record. Police may not take the phone or copy data from it without the driver's consent. They may do so with a warrant, or if they have good reason to think the phone was used in a crime. A town may pass the same rule but may not make it tougher. The Oklahoma House voted 68-21 to override the veto. The Senate did the same, so the bill became law.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 1344. It pays a drug maker to produce cheaper insulin. The act sets up a program at the State Department of Health. With money the Legislature provides, the department may help pay one or more drug makers. The drug they must work on is a fast-acting copy of an existing insulin. It has to be made in the United States. The maker must put up as much money as the state does. Before any money changes hands, the department has to sign a deal with the maker. In that deal the maker promises to sell the insulin at a low net price. The deal must also let the state take its money back if the maker does not deliver. Makers report to the department each year, and the department reports to the Governor and to legislative leaders. The Oklahoma House passed it 68-22. The Governor signed it.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 109. It makes health plans pay for cancer gene tests and scans for people at higher risk. The rule covers health plans sold or renewed in the state, including the plan for state workers. A plan must pay for a gene test that looks for an inherited change linked to cancer. That applies where the person or their family has a history of cancer. A plan must also pay for cancer scans for people at higher risk. In both cases a doctor or other provider has to order or recommend the test. The test must be useful in treating the patient and must follow national guidelines. The patient pays no deductible, copay or share of the cost. One limit applies. On a high-deductible plan linked to a health savings account, the rule starts only after the person meets the federal minimum deductible. Care that federal law counts as preventive is covered from the start. The Oklahoma House passed it 68-20. It became law without the Governor's signature.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 139. It made every school district ban student phones for one school year. For the 2025-2026 school year, each school board had to adopt a policy. The policy had to stop students using phones and personal devices on campus from the first bell to the last bell. It also had to say how the rule would be enforced. For later school years the act only says a board may adopt such a policy. So the requirement lasted one year and then became a choice. Personal devices include smart watches, smart headphones, laptops, tablets and smart glasses. Devices the school hands out for class work do not count. A board may write in exceptions. The act names two: an emergency, and a student who uses a device to track a health problem. The Oklahoma House passed it 51-39. The Governor signed it.

judgments.yea_description: Voted for Senate Bill 889. It makes hospitals publish their prices, and it stops those that do not from chasing patients for payment. Every hospital must post a computer-readable file of what it charges. The file must be free, with no login and no personal details asked for. It must list the full list price, the price agreed with each named insurer and plan, the highest and lowest agreed prices, and the cash price. The hospital must also post a plain-language price list for at least three hundred services a patient can plan ahead for. Both lists must be updated each year. The State Department of Health may check hospital websites and look into complaints. If a hospital is badly out of line, the department may demand a plan to fix it, then fine the hospital if nothing changes. The rule with real force is about debt. A hospital that was badly out of compliance on the day it treated a patient may not chase that patient for the bill. A patient who is chased anyway may sue, and collection must stop while the case runs. A hospital that a court finds was out of compliance must refund what was paid. It must also pay the patient that same amount again, cover the patient's legal costs, and clear the debt from the patient's credit record. The Oklahoma House passed it 51-38. The Governor signed it.
